title: Fresh-water species range widely and allied species occur worldwide

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Fresh-water species range widely and allied species occur worldwide

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Despite being separated by land and sea barriers, many fresh-water species of quite different classes have enormous ranges, and allied fresh-water species prevail throughout the world.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Not only have many fresh-water species, belonging to quite different classes, an enormous range, but allied species prevail in a remarkable manner throughout the world.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XII, “Geographical Distribution, continued”; section “Distribution of fresh-water productions”. Scope: fresh-water plants and animals (insects, molluscs, plants, etc.)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch12-01: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.87

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Large public distribution datasets directly support range and relatedness analyses across many freshwater groups. Coverage is broad enough to test the empirical generalization despite taxonomic gaps.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate range sizes of freshwater species across major classes and compare their distributions and phylogenetic relatedness among drainage basins worldwide. Test whether broad ranges and global prevalence of related freshwater lineages exceed matched terrestrial expectations.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Freshwater occurrence coverage is geographically uneven.

Defining 'enormous' requires class-specific thresholds.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.82
analysis feasibility: 0.88
discriminating power: 0.76
data existence: 0.96
operationalizability: 0.91

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Range size and cross-continental genus occupancy are computable for fishes and for several invertebrate and plant groups from open sources. Habitat mislabels and cryptic diversity reduce coverage below the full set of freshwater classes. A comparison with terrestrial relatives in the same clades is still a direct and feasible test of the wide-range pattern.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare geographic range sizes of freshwater species with those of related terrestrial species, and measure how often freshwater genera occur on more than one continent. Ranges no larger than terrestrial relatives, and regionally restricted freshwater allies, would count against the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Cryptic species divide ranges that look cosmopolitan under older names.

Habitat is poorly coded on many occurrence records, so freshwater sets need extra filtering.

Enormous needs a comparison group, because there is no absolute range cutoff.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Within each of three classes (insects, molluscs, flowering plants), species of fresh-water families occupy more continents than species of related terrestrial families, and fresh-water genera are more often spread over several continents than terrestrial genera.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Each pre-registered family was resolved to a GBIF backbone key and, for each of six continents, the occurrence API returned facet counts of speciesKey and genusKey (coordinates present, no geospatial issue, PRESENT, 1900-2026, fossil/living specimens excluded); a species or genus was scored present on a continent with >= 3 records. Per class and habitat set the proportion of species (P_sp) and of genera (P_gen) recorded on >= 3 continents was computed and the fresh-water and terrestrial sets compared; continents-per-species distributions were compared with one-sided Mann-Whitney tests per class and pooled.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: for every family in the fixed fresh-water and terrestrial lists, GBIF occurrence facets give the set of species and genera recorded (>= 3 records) on each of the six inhabited continents. Per class, compute P_sp = proportion of species recorded on >= 3 continents and P_gen = proportion of genera recorded on >= 3 continents, separately for the fresh-water and the terrestrial family set. SUPPORTS if in all three classes P_sp(fresh-water) > P_sp(terrestrial) AND P_gen(fresh-water) > P_gen(terrestrial), and the pooled species-level continent counts differ in the fresh-water direction (one-sided Mann-Whitney, p < 0.001).

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: REFUTES if, in at least two of the three classes, P_sp(fresh-water) <= P_sp(terrestrial) or P_gen(fresh-water) <= P_gen(terrestrial). Any other outcome is MIXED. A class with fewer than 200 species in either habitat set is dropped; with fewer than two classes remaining the result is inconclusive (underpowered).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: classes (of 3 usable) in which both the proportion of species and of genera on >= 3 continents is higher for fresh-water than for terrestrial families

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: pooled one-sided Mann-Whitney on continents per species (fresh-water > terrestrial): p=3.42e-17

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'Fresh-water species of quite different classes' is operationalised with three classes Darwin names in this section (insects, molluscs, plants), using families whose members live in fresh water, each paired with terrestrial families of the same class and, where possible, the same order (aquatic Adephaga beetles vs. Carabidae; aquatic Heteroptera vs. terrestrial Heteroptera; freshwater snails and mussels vs. land snails; aquatic angiosperm families vs. a fixed list of common terrestrial angiosperm families). 'Enormous range' is given a comparison group as both assessors demanded: a species recorded on three or more continents. 'Allied species prevail throughout the world' = the genus is recorded on three or more continents. Continents follow GBIF's continent field (derived from coordinates), excluding Antarctica. Human-mediated introductions are present in both habitat sets and cannot be separated in GBIF; this is a caveat, not a filter.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: GBIF occurrence search API (facet counts of speciesKey and genusKey per family and continent; GBIF Backbone Taxonomy for family keys)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The species-level effect in insects is small (P_sp 0.021 vs 0.018, mean continents 1.14 vs 1.12) although the genus-level effect is large (0.22 vs 0.12); the verdict for insects rests mainly on genera, which is the 'allied species prevail throughout the world' half of the claim.

Human-mediated introductions inflate multi-continent occurrence in both sets (e.g. Physa acuta, Pomacea, Sphaeriidae among fresh-water taxa; Helicidae, Achatinidae, Rosaceae and Solanaceae crops and weeds among terrestrial taxa) and cannot be separated in GBIF.

GBIF 'continent' is interpreted from coordinates; records of Oceania and islands are coarse, and species with >= 3 records on 3 continents is a crude proxy for 'enormous range'.

Family lists were fixed in advance but are a judgement sample, not the whole class; several fresh-water families (Hydrophilidae, Elmidae, Haloragaceae, Menyanthaceae) include terrestrial or amphibious members, which dilutes the contrast.

Taxonomic splitting differs between groups (e.g. cryptic diversity in fresh-water snails and mussels) and the GBIF backbone's synonymy decides what counts as one species.

GBIF is a live resource; re-running reproduces the method but counts drift as records are added.
